summary: Kole Jain walks through eight quick fixes that make interface designs look more polished. They cover tightening letter spacing on very large text, rounding nested corners correctly and smoothing corners, building a matching color palette by stepping saturation, brightness and hue in HSB, and redesigning a listing card by grouping and ranking information instead of labelling every field. He also argues for separating list items with space instead of divider lines, keeping spacing on a 4 or 8 pixel grid, and tinting backgrounds with the accent color instead of using pure white or black. For dark mode he builds depth from lighter, less saturated surface layers instead of shadows. For a design system, these give concrete starting values for display letter spacing, nested radius, palette steps, spacing base, tinted backgrounds and dark-mode surface layers.
key_ideas: Kerning (letter spacing) looks fine at small sizes, but large text over roughly 70 to 80 pixels needs tightening, around -2 to -4%.
When one rounded shape sits inside another, give the inner corner a smaller radius: outer radius minus the gap between them.
Pill shapes need no nested-radius correction because the gap is the same all the way around.
Corner smoothing (Figma's iOS corner smoothing) subtly tapers the curve before the corner, making rounded corners look rounder.
A matching palette can be built in HSB from one base color by adding about 20 saturation and removing about 10 brightness per step.
Shifting hue toward blue for darker steps improves the palette, because blues and purples read darkest and yellows and reds lightest.
Card layouts improve when obvious labels are removed, related facts are grouped, and groups are ordered by importance.
Divider lines are often redundant clutter; spacing items far enough apart usually separates them better.
If list items must sit close together, subtle alternating row backgrounds beat lines everywhere.
Consistent spacing on a 4 or 8 pixel base grid makes small components look noticeably more organized.
At large sizes, exact 8-pixel steps matter less; round to 5 or 10, or grow sizes exponentially.
Backgrounds tinted with a dark or light version of the accent color bring more color into a design than pure black or white.
In dark mode, depth comes from cards with different background colors: each layer slightly brighter and less saturated.

topics.name: Typography
topics.summary: Tighten letter spacing to about -2 to -4% on text larger than roughly 70 to 80 pixels, because fonts that look good as paragraphs can look disjointed when scaled up.

topics.name: Shape and corner radius
topics.summary: Nested corners need a smaller inner radius (outer radius minus the gap), pills need no correction, and Figma's iOS corner smoothing at maximum makes corners subtly rounder.

topics.name: Color
topics.summary: Build matching colors in HSB from a base: +20 saturation and -10 brightness per step, optionally shifting hue about 20 points toward blue for darker steps. Tint backgrounds with the accent instead of pure black or white.

topics.name: Dark mode and themes
topics.summary: Use a really dark accent-tinted background (GitHub uses a really dark blue) instead of pure black, or Tailwind's 300 as primary with 950 as background; create depth with brighter, less saturated card layers, since depth is a lot harder without shadows.

topics.name: Depth, shadows and borders

topics.name: Spacing and layout

topics.name: Visual hierarchy
topics.summary: Rank information on a card by importance, group related items, and drop labels the layout already implies.

topics.name: Cards and sections

rules.rule: Tighten letter spacing to between -2% and -4% on text larger than about 70 to 80 pixels.
rules.why: Figma handles kerning at small sizes, but large text looks disjointed with zero kerning.

rules.rule: Give a nested inner corner a smaller radius: the outer radius minus the gap between the two shapes.
rules.why: With equal radii the gap stays even on the straight edges but widens at the corner.
rules.evidence: Fixing rounded corners: 'take the outer Corner radius and subtract the distance'

rules.rule: Treat outer-radius-minus-gap as a guide and estimate the inner radius by eye, especially when the gap is larger than the outer radius (more than 30 pixels in the 30 pixel example).
rules.why: The subtraction rule breaks down once the inner corner is more than 30 pixels away, so the presenter prefers to squint and guesstimate.
rules.evidence: Fixing rounded corners: 'I just prefer to squint guesstimate'

rules.rule: Skip the nested-radius correction for pill shapes.
rules.why: A pill keeps the same distance all the way around, so you don't need to do any of this.
rules.evidence: Fixing rounded corners: 'if you got a pill shape'

rules.rule: For extra-round corners, set Figma's iOS corner smoothing to the maximum on all four corners.
rules.why: It subtly tapers the curve before the corner, which makes rounded corners look rounder.
values: iOS Corner smoothing to the max
rules.evidence: Fixing rounded corners: 'dial up the iOS Corner smoothing'

rules.rule: Derive each additional palette color from the previous one in HSB by increasing saturation by about 20 and decreasing brightness by about 10.
rules.why: This gives an objective way to get colors that match a base color without guessing.
rules.evidence: Better color palettes: 'increase our saturation by about 20'

rules.rule: When deriving a darker palette color, also slide the hue about 20 points toward blue.
rules.why: Blues and purples read darkest and yellows and reds lightest, so a darker step should move toward a darker hue; the presenter prefers this version.
rules.evidence: Better color palettes: 'we slide towards blue about 20 points'

rules.rule: Remove field labels from a card when the layout already makes each value clear, and keep labels only where values could be confused (such as check-in and check-out).
rules.why: If the UI can't imply the labels, the layout isn't doing its job; check-in and check-out keep labels so they don't get mixed up.
rules.evidence: Don't be lame with card layouts

rules.rule: Group related facts on a card and order the groups by importance, putting the least important group last.
rules.why: Name and location go together, as do cost and rating; check-in and check-out matter least because everything else must be good first.
rules.evidence: Don't be lame with card layouts: 'rank the order of importance'

rules.rule: Put a card's secondary details (such as the listing details) in a single row and add icons for context.
rules.why: Part of making the card better by being a bit more creative than listing every field.
rules.evidence: Don't be lame with card layouts: 'add some icons for some more contact'

rules.rule: Don't separate list items with divider lines unless lines are the product's chosen style; space the items far enough apart instead.
rules.why: Lines are often redundant and add clutter; enough spacing keeps items legible and clearly separate.

rules.rule: If list items must be spaced tightly, use a subtle background on alternating rows instead of lines.
rules.why: It separates rows with fewer elements than lines everywhere.
rules.evidence: Lose the lines: 'a subtle background on alternating rows'

rules.rule: Use as few elements as possible to get the point across; for example, prefer space or alternating backgrounds over lines everywhere.
rules.why: The source states the fewer elements you can use to get your point across, the better.
rules.evidence: Lose the lines: 'the fewer elements you can use to get your point across the better'

rules.rule: Build spacing on a 4 pixel or 8 pixel base grid, especially for small elements.
rules.why: It makes designs look noticeably more organized.

rules.rule: When working on an 8 pixel grid, change Figma's nudge amount from the default of 10 to eight.
rules.why: You then always stay aligned with your grid, even when making small adjustments.
rules.evidence: Keep spacing consistent: 'nudge amount change that from the default of 10 to eight'

rules.rule: For large sizes, round to the nearest 5 or 10, or if you must stay on 8, make the steps grow exponentially.
rules.why: At large sizes a small difference like 120 versus 128 is not noticeable.
rules.evidence: Keep spacing consistent: 'round to the nearest 5 or 10'

rules.rule: Use a very dark or very light version of the accent color as the background instead of pure black or pure white.
rules.why: It incorporates more color into the design; GitHub and a lot of other dark-mode software landing pages use a really dark blue instead of pure black.

rules.rule: As a shortcut, take a Tailwind color: its 50 as the light background with its 500 as the accent, or its 950 as the dark background with its 300 as the primary.
rules.why: The presenter says these pairs work for every color in the Tailwind palette.
rules.evidence: Create better backgrounds: 'copy the 50 color value and the corresponding 500'

rules.rule: In dark mode, show depth with card layers whose background is slightly brighter (about four to six) and less saturated (10 to 20) than the layer below, repeating the step for each extra layer.
rules.why: Depth is a lot harder when you have no shadows; cards with different background colors are the best way to create depth, for great depth every single time.
values: brightness slightly by about four to six

decisions.question: Should large headings keep the font's default letter spacing or be tightened?

options.name: Default (zero kerning)
options.effect: Large text can look loose and disjointed.
options.when: Normal text sizes, where Figma sorts kerning out automatically.

options.name: Tightened -2 to -4%
options.effect: Avoids large text looking disjointed; the difference is subtle side by side.
options.when: Text generally over 70 to 80 pixels.

decisions.recommendation: Tighten large text by -2 to -4%, especially given the rise of larger text on websites.

decisions.question: How should the radius of a corner nested inside another corner be set?

options.name: Same radius as the outer corner
options.effect: The gap is equal on the straight edges but increases at the corner, which looks off.
options.when: Not recommended: the source calls the widening gap an issue.

options.name: Outer radius minus the gap
options.effect: The gap stays even around the corner (30 px outer with a 10 px gap gives a 20 px inner radius).
options.when: When the gap is smaller than the outer radius.

options.name: Estimate by eye
options.effect: Works where the formula breaks down; the presenter's own preference.
options.when: When the inner corner is more than 30 pixels away (in the 30 pixel example).

options.name: No correction (pill)
options.effect: A pill keeps the same distance all the way around.
options.when: Pill-shaped elements.

decisions.recommendation: Round the inner corner less using outer radius minus the gap; estimate by eye when the gap is large; pills need nothing.

decisions.question: Should rounded corners be plain circular arcs or smoothed?

options.name: Standard rounded corners
options.effect: Regular curve into the corner.
options.when: The baseline the demo compares against.

options.name: iOS corner smoothing at maximum
options.effect: The curve tapers subtly before the corner, so corners look rounder; hard to see unless stacked side by side.
options.when: When you want to lean into the rounded-corner trend.

decisions.recommendation: Dial iOS corner smoothing to the max if you want to lean into rounded corners.
decisions.evidence: Fixing rounded corners: 'make your round corners rounder'

decisions.question: When deriving matching colors from a base color, should the hue stay fixed or shift?

options.name: Fixed hue
options.effect: Each step is the base with +20 saturation and -10 brightness; colors match but stay in one hue.
options.when: Simplest starting point.

options.name: Hue shifted toward blue
options.effect: Each darker step also slides about 20 points toward blue, which the presenter says makes the palette even better.
options.when: When you want a better palette; blues and purples tend to be the darkest hues.

decisions.recommendation: The presenter personally prefers the hue-shifted version but asks viewers to judge.

decisions.question: How should items in a list be separated?

options.name: Divider lines
options.effect: Often redundant and adds clutter to a design.
options.when: When lines are the product's deliberate style.

options.name: Space
options.effect: Items read as clearly separate with fewer elements; packing them closer makes them harder to read.
options.when: Default for lists.

options.name: Alternating row backgrounds
options.effect: Subtle stripes separate rows without lines everywhere.
options.when: When items must be spaced tightly.

decisions.recommendation: Space items apart; if they must be tight, use subtle alternating backgrounds instead of lines.

decisions.question: What base unit should spacing follow?

options.name: 4 pixel grid
options.effect: Consistent spacing that looks noticeably more organized, especially on smaller elements.
options.when: The source offers 4 or 8 without choosing.

options.name: 8 pixel grid
options.effect: Consistent spacing; set Figma's nudge amount to eight to stay aligned.
options.when: The source offers 4 or 8 without choosing.

decisions.recommendation: Use either a 4 or 8 pixel base grid; the source does not choose between them.

decisions.question: What color should the page background be?

options.name: Pure white or pure black
options.effect: Neutral, with less color in the design.
options.when: Not recommended by the source.

options.name: Accent-tinted background
options.effect: A really dark tint (GitHub uses a really dark blue) or a very light one (a site captioned 'Studio rubric' uses a very light orange) incorporates more color into the design.
options.when: Default recommendation.

options.name: Tailwind pair
options.effect: Light: 50 background with 500 accent. Dark: 950 background with 300 primary.
options.when: When you don't want to pick colors yourself.

decisions.recommendation: Use a darker or lighter version of the accent color instead of pure white or black.

decisions.question: How should cards stand out from the page in dark mode?

options.name: Shadows
options.effect: The source says depth is a lot harder in dark mode when you have no shadows.
options.when: Not the source's recommendation for dark mode.

options.name: Tonal layers
options.effect: Each card layer is slightly brighter (about four to six) and less saturated (10 to 20) than the one below; repeat for many layers, like on a dashboard.
options.when: Dark mode, especially with many layers like a dashboard.

decisions.recommendation: Use cards with different background colors, stepping brightness up and saturation down per layer.

decisions.question: How should spacing and sizes step once they get large?

options.name: Round to the nearest 5 or 10
options.effect: Looser values at large sizes, where an 8 pixel difference is not noticeable.
options.when: The presenter's usual habit for larger sizes.

options.name: Grow exponentially on the 8 pixel grid
options.effect: Stays on the grid while steps get much bigger, since 120 versus 128 makes no difference.
options.when: If you need to stick to 8 pixels.

decisions.recommendation: At larger sizes the presenter rounds to the nearest 5 or 10; if you must stay on 8, make sizes exponentially larger.
decisions.evidence: Keep spacing consistent: 'make your sizes exponentially larger'

decisions.question: How dark should the dark-mode background be?

options.name: Pure black
options.effect: Less color in the design.
options.when: Not recommended by the source.

options.name: Really dark accent tint
options.effect: A really dark blue, as on GitHub and a lot of other dark-mode software landing pages.
options.when: Default recommendation for dark mode.

options.name: Tailwind 950
options.effect: Use the 950 value as the background with 300 as the primary color.
options.when: When you don't want to pick colors yourself.

decisions.recommendation: Use a darker version of the accent color instead of pure black.
decisions.evidence: Create better backgrounds: 'a really dark blue instead of pure black'

process.detail: Start from a good base color; if you don't have one, use a color generator such as Coolors.
In Figma's color picker, change from hex to HSB so hue, saturation and brightness can be edited separately.
Leave hue alone at first; for each next color add about 20 saturation and remove about 10 brightness from the previous one.
For a richer version, slide each darker step about 20 points toward blue before applying the saturation and brightness change.

process.step: Strip implied labels from a card
process.detail: Remove labels the layout already makes clear.
Group like items (name with location, cost with rating, listing details, check-in with check-out) and order the groups by importance.
Stack name with location and cost with rating, put listing details in one row with icons for context, and give check-in and check-out their own row with labels restored.
In Figma preferences, change the nudge amount from 10 to 8 when working on an 8 pixel grid.
From the dark background, raise brightness by about four to six and lower saturation by 10 to 20 for each card layer; repeat for each additional layer.

caveats: Mobbin sponsors the video: a mid-video read about its UI library and Figma plugin, a link in the description that the presenter says helps support the channel, and a reminder at the end.

Many values are the presenter's rules of thumb, not measurements: he appears to say he eyeballs kerning (caption: 'I just ey all this') [inferred], he prefers to estimate nested radii by eye, and he personally prefers the hue-shifted palette.
The claim that the Tailwind 50/500 and 300/950 pairs work for every color is the presenter's assertion; the transcript mentions no contrast check.

Auto-caption fixes used here: 'King' as kerning, 'mobin' as Mobbin, 'coolers' as Coolors, 'contact' as context, 'read the labels' as re-add the labels, 'Tech sizes' as text sizes; 'axel grid' is read as an 8 pixel grid because the fix changes the nudge amount to 8 [inferred].
The demo palette shapes are captioned 'folder', 'band' and 'strip', and one example site as 'Studio rubric'; these names are uncertain.
Figma interface details (HSB picker, iOS corner smoothing, nudge amount default of 10) reflect Figma as of the video's publication in March 2025.
The video mentions an earlier video for the kerning example design; that video is not part of this source.
